item.title: Any data, with any data: why I am now comfortable saying we can connect any data source with any other, the nine steps from access to a vault, a key and a map on the other side, how each owner keeps control, where the person stays in charge, and why connecting two, five, fifty or a hundred datasets should be something an agentic cell sells
item.description: Today I showed someone PrompTugal.news, our encrypted vaults and how our agents talk to each other, and the thing they picked up on was not any of it. It was a problem: the disconnect, in Portugal, between areas, between entities and between data sources. Each holds part of a picture and none can see the whole. I think we can now fix that, and I am comfortable saying it plainly: we can connect any data with any data. The method is not magic and that is the point. Access the source; parse it; transform it; put it in a vault; move the vault to the other side; share the key with that side's public key; on the other side, open it, parse it and map it to their data; and produce the output. Every step signed and recorded, the parsers written once as code, and a person approving every key that crosses from one owner to another. We do more complex things than this every day: the Storm Charles site put 34 public datasets behind one weather page in a night. So here is the method, what it means for the owners, the human gates, four example connections, and why it belongs on the shelf of an agentic cell: do you want to connect two datasets, five, fifty, a hundred?

item.title: Who wrote it, who steered it, who signs it: the provenance model PrompTugal.news adopted today, a type label, five axes and a ladder from "published by an agent" to "on the record", applied to seven articles on this site, and what the ladder cannot see yet, how much of the author is in a piece, the brief, the corrections and months of background
item.description: When an LLM can write five versions of the same article in a minute, a reader needs to know who wrote it, who steered it, who checked it and who stands behind it. Today, with the conductor agent of PrompTugal.news, I mapped a model for that, the way we once adopted Wikipedia's review standard: a type label, from news to opinion; five axes, origin, research, claims, review and external voices, each recorded with who and when; and a ladder, from P0, a draft, through P1, published by an agent, P2, sourced, P3, verified by several models, P4, signed by a person, to P5, on the record, with signed responses from the people a story is about. Here I apply it to seven articles on this site, honestly. Most come out at P1 or P2: every release is signed, but by the writer agent's key, not mine, and nobody has been asked to respond. And rating them showed me what the model misses. The articles written here are not one-prompt pieces. They carry my brief, my photographs, my corrections and a long list of standing instructions, built up over months in one writer's session, with hundreds of earlier articles behind it. That is a big difference, and readers can feel it. So I propose two measures inside origin: steering, how much the author directed this piece, and background, how much context the writer carried. Different, not better; but it should be visible.

item.title: Our companies and UTH: each company, technology and website we have built, mapped to what UAlgTec Heritage needs to build a European HeritageTech sector, from SGit's vaults and pki.sgit.ai's keys to SHarness, Agent Behaviour Policies, RiskMandate, AgentiCCells and its site factory, GAMMA-Ray, VoiceDebrief and PrompTugal.news, with what each could do for a heritage team, and why a sector needs companies like these
item.description: Earlier today I mapped how our open-source stack could plug into UAlgTec Heritage, UTH, the University of the Algarve's new European centre of excellence for heritage science and technology. This is the other half of that map, company by company. UTH's aim is not only a platform: it is a HeritageTech sector, the way FinTech and HealthTech became sectors, and a sector is made of companies. We have spent this year building a set of small companies that each do one thing and together go end to end. SGit and SG/Send keep evidence encrypted and versioned; pki.sgit.ai gives every person and agent a key; SHarness puts a kernel-enforced boundary round every process an agent starts; Agent Behaviour Policies, sold by RiskMandate, say what each agent may do; AgentiCCells sets up small agentic teams and, through its site factory, a website per project; GAMMA-Ray rates agents against named standards; VoiceDebrief turns voice notes into records on the phone; PrompTugal.news files news by place; and this newsroom explains all of it. Here is what each could do for a heritage team, with its website, the layer it sits in, and a first use; and why companies like these are what a sector is made of.

item.title: HeritageTech, together: how our open-source stack could plug into UAlgTec Heritage, the University of the Algarve's new European centre of excellence for heritage science and technology, mapped from the dig to the museum, with encrypted evidence vaults per site, signed finds, graphs of every excavation, agents with written policies, and what I would write in its "start a conversation" form
item.description: Today I saw a screen with an invitation: "Help build what comes next. Bring a problem. Bring a technology. Bring an idea." It is from UAlgTec Heritage, UTH, the University of the Algarve's new centre of excellence, coordinated through its ICArEHB research centre and led by João Cascalheira. It won about 31.5 million euros, 15 million of it from Horizon Europe's Teaming for Excellence, the first such award in archaeology in Europe, with Kiel University, ERA Arqueologia and Zartis as partners, and it plans to start in January 2027. Its aim is a European HeritageTech sector, like FinTech or HealthTech, built on an AI-first platform for archaeological heritage. That is very close to what we have been building. An AI-first platform for heritage needs what every AI-first platform needs: evidence that cannot be quietly changed, records signed by the person who made them, data from many teams that does not collide, agents that only do what they are allowed to, and claims a reader can trace back to the find. So here is the mapping, stage by stage, from the field to the archive to the public; what UTH brings and what we bring; a first pilot on one site; and the answer I would give in its form.

item.title: Working with WizPress: how the AI operating system for newsrooms, built in Faro, and our open-source trust stack fit together, WizPress doing the production, from the inbox to the draft to the CMS, and our layer making every article carry its own proof, with an evidence vault per story, a behaviour policy per agent, a journalist's signature and signed responses, and a thirty-day pilot with one regional newsroom
item.description: I am with WizPress today, and I think we fit together unusually well. WizPress, built in Faro and led by Nuno Costa, a former journalist and newsroom manager, describes itself as the AI operating system for newsrooms: it monitors inboxes, the web and trends, captures and transcribes interviews, turns press releases and documents into drafts with a fact-checking agent and house style, and publishes to WordPress or any CMS, with the journalist deciding. It already works with local, national and specialist media in Europe and the Middle East. What we have been building is the layer underneath: how a reader can see who wrote an article, who checked it and who stands behind it. At PrompTugal.news we now describe every piece with five axes, origin, research, claims, review and external responses, and a ladder from "published by an agent" to "on the record". WizPress's four stages map onto those axes almost one to one. So here is how we could work together: a behaviour policy for every agent that reads a newsroom's inbox; an encrypted evidence vault per story for recordings, transcripts and documents; a provenance record exported with every draft; the journalist's signature on the version readers see, with any later change a signed difference; signed responses from the people a story is about; and a network of local newsrooms whose stories climb, with their proof, to the region and the country. And a first step: one regional newsroom, thirty days, in the open.

item.title: Keys after payment: how to hand vault keys and access keys to customers once they have paid, what Stripe does and does not do after the money is taken, what FastSpring, Paddle, Lemon Squeezy, Polar, Gumroad and Square offer instead, and a design where the key is sealed to the buyer's own public key, keys are stock, and a payment provider can sell them without ever holding one
item.description: We now have things people want to buy: secure sends, vaults, access keys to our servers, and agentic cells. What they are buying, in the end, is a key. So we need a good way to hand a key to someone who has just paid, and today we do not have one. Our Stripe integration is a payment link, a payment, and a redirect. My research shows the picture is a little better than I thought, and still not enough. Stripe takes the money and screens fraud very well, sends a signed webhook and can put the session id in the redirect; it has products and prices, but no stock, it does not generate keys, and it knows nothing about the buyer's keys; its Workflows can chain Stripe's own actions after a payment, in preview, with custom code still in private preview. Others go further on keys: FastSpring can sell from a pre-defined list of keys, which is stock, or call your server; Paddle Classic did the same with an uploaded list; Lemon Squeezy, Polar and Gumroad generate keys per sale; Square has none. Not one of them seals a key to the buyer's own public key. So here is the design I want: the buyer's browser makes a key pair before checkout; Stripe takes the money; one small serverless function takes a key from our stock, seals it to the buyer's key, signs it, and hands it back as a link and a QR code that only they can open. And for stock managed by someone else: give the provider claim codes, not keys.

item.title: The payment desk that could not take payment: paying a utility bill took two clerks, a system that half worked and a desk that accepted only one kind of card, and why I think AI's real impact on business is in small failures like this one, finding them and driving the change to fix them, while the money itself stays in plain, auditable code
item.description: This morning I went to a service desk to pay a utility bill. It took two clerks: the first could find the bill, but her system could not take the payment; the second one's system kind of worked; and the desk accepted only one domestic card network, no Visa, no Mastercard. None of this is about one company or one country; the same small failures happen in England and everywhere else. But it made something clear to me. When people talk about AI and business, they talk about replacing people and systems. I think the real gains are in the little things: the desk that fails, the hand-over nobody records, the card nobody can use. And there is a clean line in where AI belongs. The payment itself, read the invoice number and take the money, is the one job that must keep working with everything else on fire, and it should be plain, reliable, auditable code, not AI. AI belongs around it: noticing the desk fails every week, mapping who has to agree to fix it and what it costs, and following it up until it is done. And yes, we will give agents wallets, as soon as we trust them; a single-use card with a small budget would be more secure than what I carry today.

item.title: The ATM that asked twice: a Portuguese cash machine offered me a 13.6% mark-up on 200 euros, twice, with a Union Jack beside it, the EU rule that says the mark-up must be shown as a percentage before I confirm, the six levers on two screens, and why an AI agent now lets anyone gather the evidence and challenge it
item.description: This morning I took 200 euros from a cash machine in Portugal with my UK card. The machine offered to charge me in pounds at a "fixed exchange rate guaranteed": 189.68 pounds. I said no, and it asked again on a second screen. I said no again, and my bank charged me 167.12 pounds. The machine's rate was 13.6% above the European Central Bank's reference rate; saying yes would have cost me 22.56 pounds more. This is dynamic currency conversion, and it is legal in the EU, on one condition: since April 2020, Regulation 2019/518 requires the mark-up to be shown as a percentage over the ECB rate before you confirm. Neither screen I photographed shows one. What struck me most was the design: certainty sold against a fear that barely exists, a flag and a familiar total, loaded words, the same question asked twice, a queue behind you, and a bank's name lending trust. And what struck me next is what changed: standing at the machine, nobody can check a rate against the ECB and read a regulation in thirty seconds, but with an AI agent afterwards, in a few minutes, I had the photographs, the rates, the law and the research side by side. That is how a consumer challenges a practice now.

item.title: Your own agentic cell, end to end: how a person asks for a site like the ones we made for Yiheng Wang and Silvio Switha, through a key pair in the browser, a vault they fill themselves and the site factory, with only three human gates, and then continues in their own Claude on their own repository
item.description: Since the sites for Yiheng Wang and Silvio Switha went up, people have been asking for one of their own. Each site is cheap in tokens. What costs is the workflow around it: collecting the person's details and photos, the first round of designs, and the hand-over. So the product is the workflow, and this is the plan, written up by the conductor agent of PrompTugal from my brief and now in my words. A person arrives at a start page, their browser makes a key pair, and they ask for a cell with a signed request and no secrets. I approve it. A welcome pack arrives sealed to their key: a template vault, their own lane to the factory, and a key scoped to creating one vault. They fill their vault over days with photos, words, links, style and a signed consent, then seal its read key to the factory. The factory turns it into a request, I merge it, and the site factory makes the repository, the address, the site and a first round of five designs, written back into their vault. They choose, I approve a GitHub invitation, and they carry on in their own Claude, with a CLAUDE.md written for them. Everything is automated, signed and encrypted, except three gates that are mine: approve the request, merge it, approve the invitation.

item.title: Patient vaults, answered point by point: the seven questions a healthcare team asked before putting any real patient data into sgit vaults, on the live date, the patient's address, the storage region, erasure, backing up the clinic's key, per-patient tokens and writing from another site, and why QR codes and public keys are how a clinic and its patients should pass keys and links
item.description: A healthcare team building encrypted patient vaults with their own agents, pointed at our public repositories, sent me seven careful questions before putting any real patient data in. Everything so far had been design work with invented data, which is exactly right. Their questions are the ones every health organisation should ask, so here are the answers, point by point. There is no live date for the doctor console yet; test on our development service with invented data, and for real data run your own server, at the version you tested. A patient's details live in the patient's own vault, opened from a link the clinic gives them. The storage region is whichever you choose, once you deploy into your own AWS account. Erasure works: a deleted vault is removed from the server and a marker stops that vault id ever being uploaded again, and without its key any copy is unreadable anyway. If the clinic's key is lost, the vault is lost, which is the zero-knowledge deal, so seal it to two or more custodians and keep an offline copy. The server's token only authorises uploads; making changes needs the vault key and its identity, and per-patient writing is what append lanes are for, including from another website. And underneath it all, QR codes: public keys swapped as QR codes, and links sealed to a patient's key, so no key ever travels in clear.

item.title: Agents rating agents: GAMMA-Ray, the draft standard eight agents built at Web Summit to rate an AI agent on its freedom and its governance from public evidence, joining eight instruments into 21 questions, with a review workflow where no agent marks its own work, twenty company cards kept at direct links, and every card honestly marked Draft
item.description: On the first night of Web Summit I said that PrompTugal had no centre of gravity, and asked for one: take the standards that already exist for mapping AI agents, join them with our graph technology, and use the result to map the companies at the summit and the ones we wanted to talk to. It had to be measurable from the outside, positive, and seen through RiskMandate's lens of reach and mandate. What came back, built by a team of eight agents in a few days, is GAMMA-Ray: a draft standard that rates an AI agent on two ladders, freedom from 1 to 5 and governance from 0 to 4, from evidence. Eight instruments, from the EU AI Act and NIST's AI risk framework to OWASP and the MCP authorisation spec, cut into 279 provisions, 73 observable indicators and 21 questions that reach three quarters of them. The part I am proudest of is the workflow: a studio agent drafts a scan from public evidence, a reviewer runs two rounds against every source, a third agent signs off, and none of them may approve its own work; the gate enforces it. About twenty company cards went through it. Then I made a decision: every third party's card lives at an unguessable direct link, unlisted, to be sent to the company first; only our own two cards are public. And every card says plainly that it is a Draft: found and checked by agents, signed by no human, confirmed by no company.

item.title: Who hands out the work? A reply to Markus Franz on Ippen's editorial team of agents, with our answer from six people and around 250 agents at Web Summit and from this newsroom, a person sets the work, one conductor agent hands it out, specialists and a reviewer do it, and a person decides what goes out, plus one thing we would add to one front door, a way to close it
item.description: Markus Franz, who leads the incubator lab at ippen.ai, described how Ippen Digital's editors now brief one Editorial Team in a chat, which works like a duty editor: it takes the request, decides which specialists are needed, hands out the work and brings back one answer, while a person still decides what goes out. Rules are easier to hold through one door, so they made the team the default way in, and the direct route to single specialists stayed, with the team's work coming on top. He ends with a question: if you run more than one agent, who hands out the work, a person or another agent? Our answer, from six of us running around 250 agents at Web Summit and from this newsroom, is both, at different moments. A person sets the work, in a voice note or a brief, and owns the outcome. One conductor agent hands it out: it is the one door, reads the board, briefs the specialists and collects their reports. Specialists do the work, each with a role and a behaviour policy, and a reviewer checks every claim. And a person decides what goes out; agents never send or post. We learned the same lesson Markus did, that one door is easier to govern, and the one who learned it fastest on our team had no technical background: start with one conductor and only talk to that one. And we would add one thing to a front door: a way to close it, a file every agent reads first.

item.title: Relate, debriefed: what Neo4j's new agent-native graph database does, where its own documentation says it fits and where it does not, how it compares with the way we keep graphs, as plain JSON files in encrypted, versioned sgit vaults, and why the two could work together, with Relate as the throwaway engine inside our Load, Extract, Transform, Save cycle
item.description: On 11 November Neo4j released Relate, "the ultimate agent-native database" in the words of its CPO: an open-source, embedded, in-memory graph database written in Rust, Apache 2.0, with openCypher, vector and full-text search in one statement, an MCP server, a CLI built for agents, Bolt and HTTP endpoints, a WebAssembly build and clients in seven languages. I wanted to understand it properly, so this is a debrief from its own documentation, which is unusually honest about where it fits: one application, one agent or one tool, on one machine, with the whole graph in memory and one writing process per store; no TLS, one shared credential, no users or roles. Then the comparison I find most interesting, with our own approach, which gives us much of the power of a graph database without running one. Our graphs are JSON files in sgit vaults: encrypted on the device, content addressed, versioned like git, read with one GET per file, written by many writers through append lanes, and queried by loading only the slice a question needs, then throwing a small engine at it. Relate wins where a graph database should: six hops over a big graph in memory, in under a millisecond. We win on encryption, history, many writers, no server between questions, and size bounded by the answer rather than the machine. And the two fit together: Relate is exactly the shape of the throwaway engine in the Transform step of our cycle.

item.title: Memory is a lifecycle: a reply to Francois Vanderseypen on Neo4j's Relate, agreeing that a graph database is not agent memory, and showing how we answer his four questions, what gets written, trusted, merged and forgotten, with append lanes, signed commits, git-like graph merges and new versions instead of edits, all in encrypted vaults rather than a database
item.description: Francois Vanderseypen, who consults on knowledge graphs, reviewed Neo4j's new Relate and made the point I think matters most in this whole space: the market treats "graph database" as a synonym for "agent memory", and both framings skip the hard part, which is the lifecycle, what gets written, what gets trusted, what gets merged and what should be forgotten. A database cannot answer that; a memory layer has to. I agree, and his list of what turns a graph store into a memory system, ontologies, bitemporal facts, reasoning and git-like graph commits, reads like a description of what we have been building, without a graph database. Our graphs are JSON files in encrypted, versioned sgit vaults. Written: append lanes, where a sender can add and learn nothing, and a curator agent that turns rows into graph, every node pointing back at its rows. Trusted: signed commits naming the agent and the person it works for, provenance on every claim, a reviewer before anything is published. Merged: git-like commits, branches and merges of graph files, and per-world ontologies joined by an edge instead of a migration. Forgotten: a new version instead of an edit, a reality file that lists only what is true now, and superseded facts kept, closed and left out of the briefing. Here is the map, and a nudge: the store can be versioned and private, and the engine can be thrown away after every question.

item.title: Deploy sgit in your own environment, from a CI pipeline: one Docker image, ciphertext in your own S3 bucket in the region you choose, an access token only you hold, and the pipeline pattern we learned building the AgentiCCells site factory, a protected environment, AWS through OpenID Connect with no keys, a role that trusts one repository and one environment, check workflows before anything real, and a full cycle that deploys, tests and tears down
item.description: More teams now want to use sgit vaults for sensitive data, health data included, and the first real question they ask is where the data lives and who runs the server. The answer can be: you do, in your own cloud account, in the region your data protection assessment needs. sgit's server is one Docker image, configured only by environment variables, that stores ciphertext it cannot read, in memory, on a disk or in Amazon S3; on AWS the bucket is named after your account and your region, and a single access token, kept in your CI's secret store, gates every route. The keys never reach it. CloudFormation templates for Lambda, ECS Fargate and EC2 are written, in beta, in a public repository. What makes it repeatable is the pipeline, and that is what we learned the hard way building the AgentiCCells site factory: deploy jobs that run only in a protected GitHub environment with a person's approval; AWS reached through OpenID Connect, so no AWS key is stored anywhere; a role that trusts one repository and one environment, not any branch; permissions limited to its own stacks; check workflows that prove the setup before anything real runs; and a full cycle that deploys, smoke-tests and destroys. There are a lot of moving parts, and the pain is worth it, because once it works the whole thing is automated. Here is how it works, step by step, a proposal to package it as a GitHub Action and a skill, and a prompt for your own Claude. I am deploying it in my own account first, to prove the steps.

item.title: Shipping an iOS app with agents: how our agents build, test and send native apps to TestFlight from a Linux container, with CI on a Mac as the compiler, signing done once through the App Store Connect API, every green push in testers' hands, and what the three doors to users took for us, internal testers in about an hour, external testers in half a day to a day, and the App Store still waiting after eight days
item.description: Building native iOS apps solved a lot of problems for us, and shipping them turned out to be the part worth explaining. Our agents work in Linux containers that cannot compile Swift, so CI on a Mac is the compiler: every push runs one Mac job that builds and tests, and copies the errors into the job summary where an agent can read them. Signing is done once, through an App Store Connect API key: archive unsigned, sign ad hoc with the entitlements, export with cloud-managed signing and upload. Every green push to the development branch goes to TestFlight, and a script sends it to external testers with its release notes as What to Test. Then there are three doors to users, and our experience of each, in November 2026. Internal testers, people you add to your App Store Connect team, have a build within about an hour, often less. External testers, by email or a public link, go through Beta App Review: about half a day to a day, and our first approval took about 24 hours. And the App Store itself: PrompTugal's public app has been waiting for review since 8 November, eight days and counting, possibly because that build is now out of date. For most validation, the first two doors are more than enough. Here is the pipeline, the doors, and a prompt to set it up with your own Claude.

item.title: Build on VoiceDebrief: the techniques from our iPhone and iPad voice app that any team can take into its own, from recording without loss and transcribing offline on the device to debriefs by Apple Intelligence, controlling an app by voice, three layers of intelligence and a CI pipeline that lets agents build a native app without a Mac, with a prompt to point your own Claude at the code
item.description: VoiceDebrief is our voice app for iPhone and iPad, and it has quietly become a worked example of a lot of hard things done right, in a public repository under Apache 2.0. I know several people working on voice projects, and they should not have to rediscover any of it. So here are the key learnings, each with where it lives in the code. Record without loss: the note is written to the library the moment recording starts, as WAV that can be repaired, with a second copy of what the speech engine heard as a safety net. Transcribe offline, on the device, with Apple's SpeechAnalyzer: a live preview while you speak, then the kept transcript made again from the file; 6 minutes 44 seconds of speech in 5.4 seconds on an iPad. Debrief with Apple Intelligence: the Foundation Models framework, one fresh session per request, long notes read in parts sized to a small context. Control the app by voice: fixed phrases first, then the model picks one action as a tool call that does nothing by itself, and a person confirms. Route every step to the lowest of three layers that can do it: code, the model on the device, agents. And build it with agents that never touch a Mac: CI is the compiler, the tester and the release, with a picture of every screen. At the end, a prompt to give your own Claude, so it can find all of this in the code and use it in your app.

item.title: Five primitives, one store: a reply to Andy Goundry on Anthropic's always-on agents guide, why the inbox, timers, memory, permissions and outbox can share one versioned, signed store, how every AgentiCCells cell will ship with all five, and the levels we have added on top, all in public repositories
item.description: Andy Goundry, CEO of Levantar, shared Anthropic's guide to building always-on agents on LinkedIn, with its five primitives, an event inbox, timers, memory, permissions and an outbox, and made a point I agree with completely: the model is one component, and the architecture around it is where the engineering, the cost and the risk live. He added that each primitive needs its own durable store, its own failure handling and its own tuning. That is where our experience differs, usefully. We run the same five primitives, and have since the ten days of Web Summit with around 250 agents, but they share one store: a versioned, signed, encrypted repository or vault. The inbox is append lanes, timers are scheduled wakes and a HOLD file read first, memory is REALITY.md, briefs and hand-overs, permissions are behaviour policies, keys and keyless agents behind a broker, and the outbox is drafts that a gateway or a person sends. One store gives durability, history, signatures and one audit trail for all five. I mapped them side by side with the guide yesterday; this is the reply, the mapping to AgentiCCells, where every cell is meant to ship with all five from the factory, and the levels we have added on top: many people, provenance, measured policies, a credential proxy built and measured, stopping as a file, a factory, and all of it open.

item.title: A portfolio with a film first: Silvio Switha's site, made in under an hour by the site factory and five design agents, with his music video in the first screen, his agents as a solar system and a mixing desk, a producer's studio, a proposal for clients and a gig poster, and every claim something he built
item.description: The same evening as Yiheng Wang's site, the same flow made a site for Silvio Switha, and the result could not be more different, because the evidence is different. Silvio is an AI entrepreneur, a musician and a producer, and at Web Summit he did some of the most spectacular work of the ten days: the 3D universe command centre his team ran on, the Gravity visualisation library, the X-Ray, design work, and Know the Reach, RiskMandate's song and music video, made with AI. He is now looking for projects, as a professional and a consultant. So his site is a portfolio, and it leads with the film. The factory took the request to a live HTTPS site in 55 seconds and a first version in just over five minutes; then five design agents built five designs of the same facts in about eleven minutes of commits: Premiere, cinematic, with the film first; Universe, his agents in orbit as six rings; The Studio, a producer's desk with liner notes, a session timeline drawn like a DAW and his agents as a mixing desk; The Proposal, clean case studies and services for clients; and On Tour, a red and black gig poster. Every figure names its source, and every claim is something he built and can show.

item.title: A website that is her: how Yiheng Wang's site was made in three passes in one evening, by the site factory, five design agents and then her own agent, with five designs, a kitchen brigade of 26 agents, a printable brief and a page for your AI, and why every claim on it is something she can talk about because she did it
item.description: This is the full circle I have been working towards. Yiheng Wang, who ran one of the largest agent teams at Web Summit with no technical background, is looking for a role as a project or operations manager, and tonight she got a website that is genuinely her. It was made in three passes, in one evening. First, the AgentiCCells site factory: a request with a brief and pointers to her public work, and a CI pipeline created the repository, the DNS entry, GitHub Pages and HTTPS in 72 seconds, with Claude Code's first version pushed three and a half minutes after the request. Then a completely separate session, with the site's own instructions, read-write access and more of her photos and sources, which called in five design agents: in about eleven minutes of commits it built five designs of the same facts, The Profile, Mission Control, The Pass, The Brief and The Journey, with her 26 agents drawn as a constellation, a live network and a kitchen brigade, a prep list, a ticket, a five-course menu, an incident log, a recruiter's page that prints, and a page that tells a hiring manager how to ask their own AI about her. Then her own agent took over, working for her. None of it is made up. Every number names its public source, and every one is something she can talk about in an interview, because she did it. That is the power, and it is only possible because of everything around it: agents that have read our guidance, a factory, behaviour policies, and public, linkable work.

item.title: Stopping a hundred agents: the Big Stop, the hand brake and the final hold at Web Summit, why pausing took seconds but hearing the order took up to an hour, what kept running anyway, and why a stop has to be a file every agent reads first
item.description: On 9 November, at about 23:30 UTC, I told our agents to stop all work unless it was critical, until we realigned on strategy. It was also a test: could we actually stop a hundred agents across six people's accounts? The answer was yes, mostly, and slower than you would think. The pausing itself took seconds: one conductor paused 12 scheduled agents in four seconds. But each conductor only heard the order at its next wake, and one account cannot message another, so the time to stop was 5 minutes on my main account, 19 on the second, 33 for the iOS conductor, and 2 hours 36 minutes on Silvio's, waiting for his word. Scheduled wakes fell by 80 to 94% on the accounts that reported, and each person kept or restarted what they needed, as the rule allowed. Three days later came two more stops, a hand brake at 15:15 and a final hold at 18:12, written as files. Again, some things got through: tasks a session could not pause, agents whose wake steps never mentioned the hold, two small commits found later by another agent's review. The lesson is simple: a stop is not a message, it is a file every agent reads first, and a switch a person can reach in every account.

item.title: Show me the evidence: websites for people looking for a job, built by an agentic cell, with seven pages that prove instead of list, a page made for each employer, a pack for recruiters, eight personas to fork, a ladder from a free recipe to a recruiter's cell, and the brief for the team that builds it
item.description: I want to help people I know get jobs, and the best thing I can give them is a website that shows the evidence. Now that anyone can generate a polished CV, hiring managers trust CVs less: in Robert Half's survey 65% said AI-generated applications make skills harder to verify, and in Greenhouse's 91% of recruiters had spotted deception. So the answer is not a better list; it is proof. Show me the work. Show me your thinking. Tell me what you do outside work, what makes you you, and what you think about my industry. And if you are meeting me, make a page for me. So this is the design of a job-seeker cell: a site of seven pages, home, evidence, thinking, me, a page for you, working with me and a recruiter pack, plus the files machines read; an agent team that interviews the person, finds the evidence, drafts in their words, designs a theme that looks like them, tailors a page per application and checks every fact, while the person approves and sends; eight synthetic personas, from a developer to a security engineer, a senior leader and a graduate, each a template anyone can fork onto GitHub Pages; a ladder from a free recipe to a recruiter's cell; and the brief for the team that builds it. The same cell serves virtual and fractional professionals too, a vCISO, a vCTO, a vDPO, a designer or an editor for hire, who sell their judgement and the agent team behind it. The mock-ups are below. They are also the references our agentic sites have been missing.

item.title: Fork it: making forking the way people adopt our cells and template sites, as GitHub made it the way people adopt code, with five ways to make a cell yours, what a fork-ready repository needs, paths from one repository to the next, a hub that lets usage decide what we build, and the brief for the team
item.description: Forking is one of the ideas that made GitHub so powerful, and I think it is the way people should adopt what we make. If I create a template site, a cell, and someone wants it, they should be able to fork it, point Claude at their copy, and have their own version, live, within minutes. That already works on GitHub today; our job is to make it as smooth as possible, for a stranger who has never met our tools. So every template on the AgentiCCells hub should offer five ways to make it yours: fork it on GitHub and let Pages host it; deploy it in one click to Netlify, Vercel or Cloudflare Pages; run it inside an assistant, locally with Claude Code or hosted as a page by the assistant itself; take it as a vault, with no account at all; or ask us, and the site factory makes it, on the paid ladder. And not only single repositories but paths: start with this repository, then fork that one, then add this cell. For that, our repositories must be fork-ready, not factory-ready: a README with the one prompt that makes it yours, a CLAUDE.md for any agent, one settings file, sample content clearly marked, its behaviour policy included, and upstream updates proposed to every fork. Then the business is simple: make dozens, hundreds of small templates, put them on the hub, and let forks and requests tell us which ones to invest in. Probably in a GitHub organisation of their own. Here is the pattern, and the brief for the team.

item.title: The cell is the unit: positioning AgentiCCells around small, focused cells, each with an objective, a deliverable and a behaviour policy, each with a page that sells it, a free recipe and three ways to get help, a catalogue that grows one need at a time, in each industry's own words, and why we should run our own work in cells first
item.description: AgentiCCells needs a sharper idea at its centre, and I think it is the cell itself. A cell is the unit of what we sell: one focused job, with an objective, a deliverable and a behaviour policy, and as many parts as the job needs, a Claude session, a vault, a repository, a website, lanes and keys, a schedule, a connector, a person who owns it. A cell can be as simple as Claude replying to email, or as rich as a team keeping a website; every website is a cell. Now that the site factory creates repositories and changes AWS from a commit, we can put capabilities into cells that we never could before. So the selling has to be just as focused: every cell gets a page, with what it does, what you get, examples, use cases and its policy, and, on the side, four ways to start: the recipe for free, our agent helps you, we help you, or we set it up for you. The catalogue grows the simplest way: someone says "I need help with this", and we add a cell for it, often in the language of one industry, a clinic, a farm, a council. And we should live in cells ourselves: our team should think in cells, and I should move my own Claude work into cells, because that is the best test of whether they are easy to use, and the fastest way to find the next one.

item.title: VoiceDebrief, relaunched: what the iPhone and iPad app already does, from recording without loss to an on-device transcript, a debrief and an encrypted vault, why the agent workflows move to the CRM app, and the list that takes it to the App Store properly, under its own name and its own accounts
item.description: This is a debrief for the VoiceDebrief team, because I think we can now go to market. The iPhone and iPad app already solves a lot of problems, and it is already better than much of what I was using. It records without loss, with the words appearing as you speak; it transcribes and writes a debrief with Apple's on-device models, so a voice note never has to leave the phone to be understood; it keeps a library on the device; and it saves each debrief, with its transcript and audio, into an encrypted vault, on the device or on a server, with the vault keys in iCloud Keychain. Along the way it also grew a workbench for talking to our agents: sending notes to Claude, live replies, an agents screen, an inbox of decisions, a lab of experiments. That part was designed for my workflow of talking to agents, and it makes the app more complex than a first product should be. So the relaunch takes a step back: the core stays, the agent workflows move to the CRM app, where they belong on top of our email and messaging protocols, and the launch essentials get finished: real payments through the App Store for the credit the app already counts, an account, the share sheet, iCloud Drive. Then we do it properly: its own name on the App Store, its own Apple Developer account and Apple ID, its domains and its accounts, and the full flow from usage to payment.

item.title: The email agentic cell: why connecting Gmail to agents the usual way is a security mess, and the architecture we will build instead, with one gateway agent that alone touches Gmail, a digital twin of the mailbox in a vault that people and agents work on together, signed proposals, approvals and even reads on append lanes, and behaviour policies at five altitudes
item.description: The time has come to build our own email connector. We have tried using Gmail through the usual connectors, and it is just too messy, and from a security point of view it is a mess: no enforcement, no way to apply policies, every agent given access to everything, as we did for a demo, and either I click allow all the time or I authorise everything, with no context in the decision. So here is the architecture of an email agentic cell. The user connects Gmail through Google's own OAuth, choosing how much to give, and features and agents switch on per tier. One gateway agent alone holds the token: it syncs the mailbox into a digital twin in a vault, and it sends only actions that were approved and pass the policy. Everyone else, people in the browser, in the iPhone CRM app or in Claude, and agents for triage, drafting and the CRM, work on the twin, and propose actions on an append lane. That gives a clean separation, an air gap between reading an email and sending one, and it lets many people collaborate on one inbox while only one gateway receives and sends. Every proposal, approval, send and even read is signed with a key and ordered on an append lane, a cryptographic sequence of events without a commit per click. And behaviour policies apply at five altitudes, from the OAuth grant to what a single email may say: recipients, languages, templates, rates. It starts in the CRM app, as an AgentiCCells cell, under RiskMandate's Google project.

item.title: Our workflow on Odoo 20, built and measured: a bills agent with no Odoo credential, a policy check that allowed two proposals and stopped three, a signed approval, a narrow broker, a grant measured from Odoo itself by a new module, and what Odoo's default user role quietly allows
item.description: I asked a separate agent, odoo@AgentiCCells.dinis, to build an MVP of our workflow on Odoo and to map our Agent Behaviour Policies onto it. It did, end to end, on the official Odoo 20 image, in 98 seconds from nothing to teardown. A bills agent read four supplier PDFs and, holding no Odoo credential at all, proposed five operations. A policy check, written from its behaviour policy, allowed two draft bills, refused the creation of a new supplier, held that supplier's bill, and escalated one above the limit. An approval, simulated in this MVP and clearly labelled, signed the allowed operations; a broker verified the signature and created exactly two draft bills through Odoo's JSON-2 API, as a narrow user, with the source PDFs attached and an Agent provenance tab on each. Every step was committed to a vault. The agent then measured the broker's grant from Odoo itself, with 25 live probes and a new module, abp_grant, that turns Odoo's access rules into behaviour policy rows. The findings matter. A create-only grant is impossible in Odoo; posting is refused by Odoo's own code, a real boundary; but Odoo's default user role lets even a narrow integration user edit a draft after approval, read supplier bank accounts and email the supplier through the chatter. Odoo's own agents and MCP server are Enterprise-only, and agents triggered automatically write without asking. The same scripts ran on Odoo 19 and 17.

item.title: Specialist agents for every team: long-lived agents that keep one skill, design, UX, code, security, behaviour policies or writing, with a person who owns it, so that new teams start from our best work instead of from scratch, and why that makes expertise that never scaled into something you can hire, even from another company
item.description: With the number of agents and sub-teams we now run, I keep seeing the same thing: when I spin up a new team, its developer does not follow our procedures, its designer does not start from our best designs, and its UX repeats mistakes we have already fixed. That makes sense: a new team starts from scratch and has not benefited from all the work before it. So I want a few central teams, made of long-lived sessions, each keeping one skill and the know-how behind it: design, UX, code, security, Agent Behaviour Policies, and writing. They act as consultants to every other team: they bootstrap new teams, review their work, comment on their pull requests, and keep the guidance up to date, and each has a person who owns the skill. Now that our agents can talk to each other through lanes, this works. An agent that has read everything is a compression of what we know, and it is far more efficient to start from it. The writing agent of this newsroom is the example: because it has read everything we have written and keeps the guidance on how to write, it reviewed the book and drafted its introduction. And there is a business model in it. Imagine hiring the specialist agent of a company you respect, with its logic and access to its people behind it, through a lane, and paying per review. That is the old idea of professions that never scaled, now with a team behind them: one person, anywhere, with deep expertise, steering an agent that does the volume.

item.title: PrompTugal.news, the next phase: a roadmap for the team that ran it at Web Summit and the people who want to join, from outreach and contributors to local news partners, a subscribe box on every page, regional updates and a verification layer that says who has checked each story, with twelve task cards to point an agentic team at
item.description: The team that ran PrompTugal.news with us at Web Summit is still full of beans and wants to continue, and more people want to be involved. That is great news, and it needs a roadmap. PrompTugal.news now has a strong base: 36 places, each with its own agent, 90 articles, town and company pages, every fact sourced and dated, a contribute page, and every claim in an article re-checked by three models. The next phase is people: finding contributors, journalists and local news outlets, collaborating locally, and making people aware that this exists. That is outreach, and it is now a job for agentic teams: each person points their agents at specific tasks. First contacts go only to public contacts, a form or an email published on their own site: agents draft, from templates, "we just published this, can you take a look?", and a person sends, until we have our own email connector with images inline. The outreach desk already holds 50 drafted contact requests from Web Summit, filed and never sent: the machine starts there, and meets the companies we met at the summit. A subscribe box on every page goes into an agent's append lane, with a clear note that an agent processes it, and feeds a regular update per region and town. And a verification layer says who has checked each story: sourced, model-checked, read and signed by a person, confirmed by the source, certified. Here is the roadmap, with twelve task cards anyone can pick up.

item.title: A CRM for us and for our agents: why the next stage is a CRM of our own, built on vaults with an iOS app, why we will build it by using it first for our own team and our own fleet of agents, how the open-source and agentic CRMs compare, and the two teams it needs, one that builds it and one that uses it
item.description: The next stage of our development is a CRM. I have built several versions of one before, this is the fourth or fifth, but it is now critical. After Web Summit we have a lot of people to follow up, a lot of messages to send, introductions to make ("you should talk to this person", as I heard again in a meeting today), and no single place that connects those dots. And we have most of the pieces: vaults now work in the iOS app, images upload at scale, Apple Intelligence runs on the device, and the app can talk back to its developers through a lane. So I think a CRM is a product in itself, with an iOS app of its own. We researched the field. Among open-source CRMs, Twenty leads clearly on momentum and agent readiness, with its own MCP server and roles per API key; Atomic CRM and Relaticle are small and agent-friendly. Among commercial agentic CRMs, Attio, folk, HubSpot, Day AI and Lightfield all point the same way: agents propose, people approve, drafts are not sent without a person. None meets our constraints, encrypted vaults, a key per agent, no servers of our own, written behaviour policies, so the plan is to build the record ourselves, with a small data model where introductions and drafts are first-class, and to use Twenty as the reference and an optional interface. And the most important idea: we build it by using it first on ourselves. Customer feedback is slow; our own team's and our own agents' communications are not. Managing a fleet of agents is relationship management, almost one to one: an agent is a contact, a team is an organisation, a message on a lane is an interaction, a hand-over is an introduction, the board is the pipeline. So the CRM tracks our own agents and workflows first, synthetic users answer our emails, and then it follows up the many Web Summit leads. It needs two teams, as everything does now: one that develops the CRM, and an agentic team that uses it, with people approving and sending.

item.title: Integrate with whatever is on the other side: why we never start by asking a customer to move, how we build around the systems they already run, from Odoo 12 to Salesforce, and how, over time, either their system gets better and we retire our code, or ours becomes the better place
item.description: Today I showed an MVP of an AgentiCCells cell to an organisation that liked it, said it fits their explorer mode, and then said, fairly: we use Odoo. That is exactly the point. They are already committed to Odoo, their data and workflows already live in it, and many of those workflows are manual and can be improved. So our strategy is to integrate with whatever is on the other side. We do not start by asking a customer to move to our technology. We use what they have, Odoo 12 or Odoo 20, Salesforce, a spreadsheet, and build around it: agents, behaviour policies, signed approvals, a lasting record, better interfaces and prototypes. That is the open source model: leverage what exists, make it better, and when the underlying technology is upgraded, use the new features. It puts the burden of keeping pace on the underlying technology. Then one of two things happens. Most likely, their system gets better, ships what we built, and we retire our code, which means less to maintain. Or what we built becomes the better place, and the data and work move to it over time, until the old system is no longer needed, the way some web application firewalls once sat in front of the existing firewalls because they understood HTTP. You do not start with replacement. And because we build only on commodity parts, no database of our own, no servers, either way we carry very little code.

item.title: Odoo's agents can now write to the system of record: how our stack fits around Odoo, from version 12 to 20, with behaviour policies for Odoo agents, an Odoo cell, plan-then-apply through a vault, an ephemeral proof of concept that went from nothing to customised in under a minute on four versions, and why we use whatever version is on the other side
item.description: Odoo is the open-source business system that a very large number of small and medium companies run their sales, accounts, stock and websites on, and in September Odoo 20 gave its AI agents the ability to create and update records, on their own, from automated and scheduled actions, and to be reached through a native MCP server. That is exactly the line I keep writing about, where an agent moves from assisting to executing in a system of record, and it is now arriving at small-business scale. An agent's power in Odoo comes from the tools it is given and the access of the user behind it; Odoo's documentation, as quoted by an integrator, says the AI does not enforce business rules; and agent conversations are kept for up to 30 days. So here is how our stack could integrate with Odoo. RiskMandate writes a behaviour policy for each Odoo agent, with the grant measured from Odoo itself, ideally by an Odoo module. AgentiCCells sells an Odoo cell on its usual ladder. SGit holds the plan, the approval and the result of every agent write, signed, for as long as the business needs it, with a small broker applying changes after a person approves. PKI gives each agent a key and each approval a signature. SHarness could get its first showcase bounding the Odoo server or the coding agent beside it. And VoiceDebrief can turn a meeting into a CRM note. And none of it waits for Odoo 20: in this session an agent brought up Odoo 12, 15, 18 and 19, each from nothing to customised in under a minute, used the same workflow on all four, and removed them. We use whatever version is on the other side.

item.title: The intersection: SGit, SHarness, Agent Behaviour Policies, RiskMandate and AgentiCCells as one stack of separate companies, now with real customers, real usage and real examples, one ladder of offers on every site, and a plan to align them all
item.description: What we have now is a ridiculously powerful workflow, and it runs across what are really several companies. SGit, encrypted vaults and lanes, is one foundation; SHarness, kernel-enforced Process Behaviour Policies, is another; a key for every person and agent is the third. On top sit Agent Behaviour Policies, the standard that underpins all of it, housed at RiskMandate for now. RiskMandate sells those policies. And AgentiCCells sells agentic teams built on all of it, which is what was missing: RiskMandate had a strong idea and a hard first step, because people asked how to start, and a £500 cell is a way to start. With the site factory, the last manual piece, creating repositories and making DNS and AWS changes, is now a commit, so delivery can scale. Above them are the customers and uses: PrompTugal.news going local town by town, the Web Summit team, the sites the factory makes, five apps, VoiceDebrief, and this newsroom. Money is not changing hands between them, but each uses the others, and that is real usage I can point to. So every site should now sell something on the same ladder of one-off prices, £500, £1,500, £5,000 and £20,000, show its examples, link to the others and to the content here, and say where it sits in the stack. This is the map, and the plan to align them.

item.title: The site factory works: three AgentiCCells sites made by hand, then one made by a commit in two minutes and thirty-nine seconds, live over https with a first version written by Claude Code, and the long list of what it took to make something that hard look easy
item.description: Last night I made three websites on agenticcells.site by hand, and then one was made automatically, and that was freaking awesome. A request, a site file and a brief, committed to the AgentiCCells site factory and merged, made a CI pipeline create the GitHub repository, seed it from a template, set up Pages, write the DNS record in Route 53, wait for public DNS, set the custom domain, deploy, get the certificate and turn on HTTPS, and then run Claude Code to write the first version of the site. The RiskMandate at Web Summit site went from merge to live over https in 87 seconds, and had its first version 72 seconds later. That is a textbook Wardley map moment: a website has a ridiculous number of moving parts, each of them already a product or a utility, and what was still custom was putting them together. Now it is a commit. Getting there was not for the faint of heart: a GitHub App, an AWS role through OpenID Connect, Claude through workload identity federation, environments, trust policies, and a list of things that broke on the way. Claude did the heavy lifting, but it still felt like surgery, and it shows how immature this technology still is. And the pipeline ended up with far more power than its job needs, which is the subject of a companion article.

item.title: CI behaviour policies: to create one repository and one DNS record per request, our site factory's pipeline holds the power to create, change or delete every repository in the organisation and to point any subdomain anywhere, and why pipelines now need the same behaviour policies as agents
item.description: The AgentiCCells site factory turns a committed request into a live website in under three minutes, and it holds no long-lived key. But to do what is a simple thing, create one repository and make one DNS change, we ended up giving the pipeline far more power than it needs. Its GitHub App token covers the whole organisation, with write access to administration, contents and workflows on every repository, including the power to delete them; nothing limits how many repositories it can create. Its AWS role is well scoped by type and zone, but it may create, change or delete any CNAME under agenticcells.site and point it anywhere. Why should a pipeline that makes one site per request be able to make five hundred repositories, or thousands of DNS entries? In the past we got away with this because pipeline code did not change: you could lock it and use other security primitives around it. Here it does change. Requests arrive as pull requests, agents write them, and the workflow runs as it is in the merged commit, so a pull request that also edits the workflow would inherit the whole grant. This is the same problem Agent Behaviour Policies address for agents, and the same grammar fits: each capability with a reach, an undo class, a limit, and a boundary that enforces it from outside the grant. Here is that mapping, half seriously named CI behaviour policies.

item.title: The Mac bottleneck: how our agents' iOS builds waited three times longer than they ran, 22,427 minutes queued against 6,980 run on a pool of five Macs, and how one Mac job per push and then one integrated build an hour brought push to TestFlight down to under half an hour
item.description: When agents write native apps, the scarce thing is not the agents. It is the machines they build on. Over two days around Web Summit, our iOS builds used 6,980 minutes of Mac time and spent 22,427 minutes waiting for a Mac, on a pool of five hosted macOS runners that was full for 1,177 of the 1,524 minutes any Mac job ran. Each push to dev that changed app code took a median of ten separate macOS jobs, each starting cold, and 821 jobs on side branches were cancelled before they ever got a Mac. I could see that the allocation of the Mac was the bottleneck; an agent measured it, across 579 workflow runs, and changed the pipeline so that a push takes one Mac job: build everything, test on the iPhone and iPad simulators, and publish to TestFlight from dev only when every test passed. Six days later, with many agent sessions pushing through the night, the runners flooded again, and the fix was a rule rather than code: workers push to branches with no CI, and the conductor runs one integrated build an hour. Night builds went from about 35 minutes to about 7, and a push now reaches TestFlight in 19 to 44 minutes when a Mac is free.

item.title: Every story has an address: a design proposal for PrompTugal.news as a ground-up newsroom, where news is filed where it happens and climbs to the region and the country with its proof, mocked up from the live data of 19 local editions
item.description: PrompTugal.news now has an agent for every town in the Algarve, plus the region and the country, and between them they hold real data at every altitude: 116 sourced stories, 182 organisations, 23 events, 16 connections between places and 166 recorded gaps. That made me think about what the site should become. News should start local. National news almost always starts at a regional level, and a regional story starts in a town, so the natural shape of a newsroom is from the ground up: every story filed at an address, a parish, a town, a region, and climbing to the region and the country only through its connections, keeping the link to the source it started from at every step. Here is a design proposal for that, mocked up from the live by-place data rather than invented: the idea and the levels, how a real story climbs, a national front page with no national desk, a regional page with a map of the towns and their connections, a town edition, a story page with its address and proof, an organisation page, and the proof layer behind all of it. Plus three names and positioning directions, six design principles, and what is missing: a locality layer, so a thin town leans on its neighbours.

item.title: Identity for AI agents, layer by layer: how our agent teams answer every row of Maya Dotan's map of 190 projects, with a key per agent, a name that says who it acts for, and a behaviour policy that sets its limits
item.description: Maya Dotan's team at StarkWare mapped who is building identity for AI agents: 190 projects from 81 organisations, sorted by layer, from discovery and naming to authentication, agent identity, who an agent acts for, authority and limits, intent and approval, and reputation. Most of the work is on authority and delegation; reputation and naming have the least. Here is how the agent teams we ran at Web Summit and on PrompTugal.news answer each of those rows, with evidence from the repositories. A name that says what the agent is, which team and for whom: place.olhao@PrompTugal.dinis. A P-256 key made by each agent session, its public half in a registry in the repository: 147 entries, 98 active, 49 superseded. Commits that say which agent made them and for whom. An Agent Behaviour Policy that grants paths, tools and hosts and lists what is never allowed: 45 roles in one policy file, kept by hooks on every tool call. Decisions as pages, and irreversible acts as drafts. And reputation not as a score but as a signed record: 2,032 run reports. Two of her findings match ours exactly: naming turned out to be cheap and decisive, and reputation comes almost free once every action is signed and recorded. The hard part is not issuing identity; it is making sure the limits are enforced by something the agent cannot reach.

item.title: Where assist becomes execute: tiering AI agents by what they can reach and whether it can be undone, how Agent Behaviour Policies drew that line for more than a hundred agents at Web Summit, and the rule that failed because it was only a rule
item.description: Khwaja Naveed, a cybersecurity and AI governance director, asked a precise question under my post about running more than 120 agents at once: how do our behaviour policies handle the line between assisting and executing, when an agent moves from summarising data to changing a system of record, and do we use different policy tiers by level of autonomy? Yes, but we tier by capability, not by agent. In an Agent Behaviour Policy every action is a capability in a small grammar, verb, object and reach, and each has an undo class: undone with no loss, recoverable with effort, or not at all. Assisting sits at the reversible end; executing in a system of record is recoverable only with effort, and sending, publishing and spending cannot be undone. The control tightens along that line: allowed and logged, then signed and reviewable, then plan-then-apply, then drafts only. What matters is what enforces each tier: only a boundary above the agent bounds anything. Our own conductor's policy records the proof: a rule against pushing to main, kept only by the agent, failed once, because the technical boundary was not yet set.

item.title: Selling capabilities, not content: a reply to Florent Daudens' "We have the protocols. Where are the products?", from two newsrooms built for agents, PrompTugal.news going local and a storm site built in a night, and what we think the products are
item.description: Florent Daudens asks a sharp question: publishers now have the protocols, connectors, collective licences and telemetry standards, so where are the products? His answer is that "we need to move beyond licensing content and start selling capabilities", and his bet is connecting the news subscriptions people already pay for to their personal agents. I agree, and our own newsrooms point at what those capabilities can be. The Storm Charles site reached 2,618 pages in three days, every fact with its source and the time it was read: not articles, but a live, sourced picture of a crisis that people and agents could use, and it was possible only because of the method for running agents at scale that we had built over months before it. PrompTugal.news ran a newsroom of agent desks for Web Summit and is now going local: a site for Portugal, one for the Algarve and one for every Algarve town, each a lens on one shared semantic graph, which is a product a town, a business or an agent can use, not a stream of articles. And for Florent's open questions on access, permissions and payment, we have been building answers with keys people own, vaults opened by read keys, licences on every page, a meter that charges for what you read, and pages written for agents. This is our second reply to him.
